title: Lower back rounding: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
summary: A case-by-case argument on lower and upper back rounding in squats and deadlifts, built off Geoffrey Verity Schofield's video. Rounding is neither absolutely dangerous nor absolutely safe: risk only exists for a specific load, lift and individual. The real trap is thoracic rounding, because the spine gives up in stages and thoracic rounding drags the lumbar spine into rounding. For bodybuilders, chasing extra load by rounding is self-defeating anyway: it shifts work away from the legs and costs gains.

claims.claim: Back rounding is mainly discussed on lower-body lifts (squats and deadlifts and their variations) because the lower back can only round when you are standing or horizontal; you rarely hear about it on the bench press.
Back rounding usually happens on the positive (concentric) phase because the structure gives way to the weight: the body reshapes itself around the bar to get the weight up.

Good-morning squats and immediately bending over in deadlifts are usually not a choice: the body lacks the ability to stay upright against that weight, so it is the only option it has - which is why this rounding is mostly a correctable technical issue, though people hate being told to retrain themselves.

Consensus (back rounding is an injury risk) creates a void for dissenting opinions; YouTube fitness is a pendulum that swings between extremes and rarely rests in the middle, which is where objective truth lies.

There is no absolute injury risk attached to upper or lower back rounding: it only exists for a certain intensity, lift and person. Same person and lift with more load becomes dangerous; switch the person or the lift at the same load and it becomes dangerous too.

He is personally an advocate of perfect form and never rounds his back, but admits this bias partly comes from his proportions; everyone should strive toward the most effective technique that prevents injury best.

If there is one moment you never want form breakdown, it is on heavy weight - that is when load is highest and the structure most compromised; it is much better to have bad form on light lifts and good form on heavy lifts.

Many people let form compromise on heavy lifts because it lets them lift more, but that does not prove compromised form is the most effective way to move the weight - it is often just animalistic release, forgetting everything and struggling against the bar.
Form relativism (there is no such thing as bad form) destroys the ability to correct form: if nothing is bad, there is no reason to retrain anyone - the pendulum has swung so much it became a circle.

Stress is not the enemy: lifting stresses muscles and tendons and that is what makes muscle grow and tendons reinforce; you want to maximize stress on the muscle and minimize it on tendons, and there is a sweet spot - go too extreme and you snap.

Tendonitis recovery also requires stress: saying no stress at all will not heal a tendon, you have to load it progressively until it recovers; stress levels are manipulated through volume and intensity.
Life parallel: stress is necessary - never being stressed leaves you bored and depressed, while too much stress breaks you; the dose makes the poison.

The but-elite-X-deadlifts-with-a-rounded-back argument is invalid: a top powerlifter pulling 900 lbs raw has the structure, body connection, technique and knowledge that a 300-lb deadlifter lacks, so what is fine at high load for him is not automatically fine at low load for you.

Konstantin Konstantinovs, his favorite deadlifter of all time, deadlifted with a rounded upper back but had the core thickness of an ox - no belt, slapping his abs and saying this is my belt; such an outlier of core rigidity cannot be used as an argument for average lifters.

Olympic weightlifters do rounded-back deadlifts intentionally, with light fully controllable weight, to recruit the most erectors possible - at no point entering an injury-risk range because they know what they are doing.

He never lets the practices of elites seep into what he teaches because novices will run with them: given the choice between fixing their own technique and copying a Chinese weightlifting champion, lazy people always take the excuse, and it is the job of the knowledgeable to bar that path.

Depending on height, limb lengths and proportions, you cannot fight certain angles; multiple techniques exist for every lift so outliers can find a near-universal variant that lets them train for years without getting hurt.

Above six feet you are already a minority, above 6'2" even more so - most YouTube fitness advice does not apply to very tall lifters, who may need sumo or block pulls and should not be shamed by the conventional-deadlift-only-or-you're-not-a-man dogma.
Block pulls often provide more total range of motion than some lifters' full-range deadlifts anyway, so who cares - do what works for you.
Genetic gifts and curses: muscle bellies and testosterone count matter, but the most important genetic factor is your structure's ability to handle and resist stress.

His lower back is made of metal: he can do pause reps and heavy deadlifts at high frequency and has never had lower back pain - but he refuses to preach his methods as a bulletproof-back formula because it is clearly genetic.

Spine shape affects disc integrity: research found certain spine shapes are extremely resistant to torsion and stress while others are basically made to snap, so advice from someone with a strong spine does not transfer to you.
Some techniques only work if you have the structure for them - like the flicker jab of the Philadelphia guard in boxing, which only suits long-armed boxers; take technical cues with a grain of salt.

He preaches deadlifting with a neutral spine and very deep hips; not everyone can copy his technique, but everyone should strive for knee flexion, strong hip involvement (which triggers the posterior chain) and as neutral a back as possible.

Thoracic (upper back) rounding receives less stress than lumbar rounding because the lumbar spine sits smack in the middle of the loaded structure, while the upper back gets less due to the repartition of the discs - so rounded-upper-back-is-fine is an argument he can receive.

Thoracic rounding causes lumbar rounding in people who don't know what they're doing: you can find clips of a neutral lumbar spine with a rounded upper back (KK did that), but you cannot find the reverse - a rounded lower back with a straight thoracic spine is an impossibility, because the spine gives up in stages, starting with the shoulders protracting.

The spine is a unit: even if thoracic rounding were harmless in itself, allowing it while being unable to prevent lumbar rounding is dangerous - and posture degenerates rep by rep, so the toughest reps where you should be tightest are exactly when you are most rounded and get snapped up.

If you are a bodybuilder, I round my upper back because I lift more that way misunderstands the sport: lifting heavy is not the goal, triggering muscle growth is; rounding is merely a mechanical advantage that lets the bar shoot off the floor at its hardest point.

The difference between controlling your body and letting it dictate the pace: he could round his upper back on every deadlift but instead tells himself to stay tight and fight through it; bodybuilders should have the cleanest form of all to direct tonnage effectively.
The more you round the back the more the back engages in the lift, and tonnage leaks away from the legs - yet the deadlift should be growing your glutes and hamstrings.

Fishing rod deadlift: with the spine exaggeratedly rounded from the start, the legs shoot straight immediately; by lockout the knees and hips are locked but the shoulders and thoracic extension are not, leaving you to uncoil the back with the legs out of the movement - a weak position where people hitch because the power source is gone.
In a proper deadlift the bar goes up as the legs straighten and everything locks at the same time.
Beyond the injury question, rounding your back teaches a movement pattern that might not hurt you now but will definitely hurt your muscular gains - and gains are what matter on this channel.

exercises.name: Deadlift
cues: maintain knee flexion and strong hip involvement to trigger the posterior chain
stay tight and fight through the grind instead of letting the back round
exercises.why: directs tonnage to the posterior chain and protects the spine; rounding shifts work to the back and starves the legs of growth

exercises.name: Sumo deadlift
cues: a valid substitution when your proportions do not suit conventional
exercises.why: tall lifters without conventional proportions can save their backs and still train hard

exercises.name: Block pull
cues: legitimate variation for lifters whose structure does not allow conventional
exercises.why: often more range of motion than some people's full deadlifts; lets you keep pulling without forcing bad positions

exercises.name: Good-morning squat (form error)
cues: recognize it as the body's only option when thoracic extension fails in the hole
exercises.why: criticised pattern: it is a compromise that sacrifices quad growth and must be retrained, not accepted

exercises.name: Rounded-back deadlift (Olympic lifter style)
cues: only intentional, with light fully controllable weight, to bias the erectors
exercises.why: elites do it deliberately inside a controlled range; novices copying it round unintentionally and get hurt
